scenes.title: Cost Anomaly Detection
scenes.narration: This slide shows how AWS Cost Anomaly Detection looks for unusual spending patterns. Historical billing data establishes an expected cost range, and a new observation is compared against that learned baseline. When a service, linked account, tag or defined cost category departs meaningfully from expectation, the service identifies an anomaly and highlights contributing dimensions. The sample chart and impact percentages illustrate the mechanism; they are not current charges in a real account. On the right, an investigator sees the start and end dates, estimated financial impact and likely drivers. Choose a monitoring scope that matches ownership boundaries, such as a production account or one expensive inference-related service. Notifications depend on configured impact thresholds and subscriptions. An anomaly is not automatically a security incident or a billing error: a legitimate product launch might explain a higher spend. Equally, an apparently small anomaly may be critical for a tiny development account. This detection is an investigative signal, not a hard real-time spending cap, and billing-data availability may lag behind live usage.

scenes.title: Anomaly alerts and triage
scenes.narration: The workflow starts by selecting a cost monitor, configuring alert frequency and impact thresholds, then receiving notifications. Individual alerts or summary digests can reach the appropriate response team. Follow the example alert into Cost Explorer, where the operator filters by service, Region, usage type and linked account to identify what increased. In the illustrative report, EC2 accounts for a larger cost rise than a small RDS change, so the investigation should focus there first. Compare actual and expected spend, then review resource launches, deployment activity, pricing changes and workload usage before taking action. The slide calls out billing-data latency: recently created resources may not yet appear in the cost report. It also distinguishes anomaly detection from a fixed AWS Budget threshold. A learned baseline asks whether behavior changed unexpectedly; a budget asks whether spending has crossed a defined limit. After root-cause analysis, use a controlled fix such as rightsizing, stopping a forgotten test resource or adjusting deployment limits, and document prevention. Never automatically terminate production infrastructure merely because an anomaly was detected.
